content_voiceover: These two tables catalog gene therapy programs using adeno-associated virus, or AAV, vectors for hemophilia A and B. Gene therapy works by delivering a functional copy of the deficient clotting factor gene, packaged in an AAV capsid, so the patient's own liver cells start producing factor VIII or factor IX endogenously, ideally eliminating the need for chronic factor replacement. For hemophilia A, in the top table, valoctocogene roxaparvovec, brand name Roctavian, using an AAV5 vector with a B domain deleted factor VIII transgene from BioMarin, has already received European Medicines Agency approval, while several other candidates like giroctocogene fitelparvovec and dirloctocogene samoparvovec remain in earlier phases. For hemophilia B, in the bottom table, etranacogene dezaparvovec, which uses the Padua variant of factor IX, a hyperfunctional mutant, delivered via AAV5, has achieved FDA approval from CSL Behring. The Padua variant is a key detail, since that single amino acid substitution gives factor IX roughly eight to twelve times normal specific activity, which is why it was chosen as the transgene payload. Note that hemophilia B gene therapy programs are generally a bit further along than hemophilia A ones, partly because the factor IX gene is much smaller and easier to package into the AAV vector than factor VIII.
keypoints: AAV vectors deliver functional factor VIII or IX genes directly into liver cells
Valoctocogene roxaparvovec (Roctavian) for hemophilia A is EMA approved, uses AAV5
Etranacogene dezaparvovec for hemophilia B is FDA approved, uses the hyperfunctional Padua factor IX variant
Hemophilia B gene therapy is more advanced partly because factor IX is a much smaller gene to package
keypoint_voiceover: Remember the two approved gene therapies, Roctavian for hemophilia A using AAV5 factor VIII, and etranacogene dezaparvovec for hemophilia B using the Padua variant of factor IX, which is hyperfunctional.
